Tesla Buying Board

Tesla Buying Board

Ranked by bang for the buck, for Shawn in Bourbonnais, IL. Prices checked on Tesla.com and cars.com on Thursday, November 5, 2026 (first version October 11; refreshed every day around 12:15 PM). Used rows are Tesla's own pre-owned inventory with a clean history. Cars sell within days, so a link may be gone by the time you click. Every car now shows how long it has been watched and every price cut since.

The short answer: buy a 2023 Tesla from Tesla's own used inventory. Don't lease.

The federal tax credit is gone, so leases are no longer subsidized, and the Illinois $2,000 rebate only pays if you buy. A clean 2023 Model 3 from Tesla's Batavia store costs $28,800 (about $26,800 after the Illinois rebate), carries battery coverage into 2031, and Tesla adds its own 1-year/10,000-mile used warranty. Clean dealer 2021 to 2023 Model 3s run $22,300 to $24,900, and clean Model Ys start near $23,000. A new Model Y Standard is $41,630 and loses roughly $8,000 the first year, which is money the 2023 owner already lost for you.

Shopping on a tight budget? The Under $15k tab ranks the cheapest Teslas in the country by price for battery left (dollars per mile of range). Pick the tab for the car you want, or the combined power rank to see both models head to head. Each list has its own benchmark: the #1 deal on that list sets the bar, every other deal shows its score against it, and cars that meet or beat the bar turn yellow.

Best time to buy: December 15 to 31, 2026

Three things line up in those two weeks:

  • Tesla's year-end push. Tesla discounts hardest in the last 10 to 14 days of a quarter, and the last quarter of the year is the biggest. Last December it offered 0% financing, free upgrades on inventory cars and $0-down leases, and its used cars keep getting marked down until they sell (the Mechanicsburg Model 3 was cut four times in nine days).
  • Used prices hit their yearly low. Used-car prices track the weather: they fall from November and bottom out between December 31 and February 28 (iSeeCars). Fewer people shop for an electric car in a Chicago winter.
  • Last confirmed chance for the Illinois $2,000 rebate. The current application window closes December 31, 2026 , and the state has not announced a 2027 window. It only applies to cars bought from an Illinois dealer.

Second-best: January and February 2027, when used prices are lowest, but the rebate is uncertain and Tesla's next push is not until March 18 to 31. Worst: spring and early summer, when tax refunds bring buyers back. Before December: get a credit-union pre-approval and your Jeep offers lined up, so you can move the day the right car shows up. Buy sooner only if the watch below says YES.

Reality check from the daily log (Nov 5): the typical asking price has barely moved since Oct 25 (+0.2%), so waiting alone has not made cars cheaper yet. Single cars do get cheaper every day they sit, then sell, and a fresh car takes the spot at a fresh price. So the deal comes from catching one car late in its cuts, in any week. The cut clock on each Tesla-store car, and the table on the Power rank tab, show the odds.

Can't-say-no watch

Why $55 per mile of range: a new Model Y Standard costs about $130 for each mile of range, a 3-year-old Tesla from Tesla about $100 to $140, and the cheapest high-mile cars about $40 to $60. Paying $55 or less means getting range at well under half the new-car price; pairing it with battery warranty keeps worn-out cars from winning.

Nothing clears the can't-say-no bar today. You will see a green YES here (and get a phone alert) the day something does.

Power rank: every Model 3 and Model Y on this board, together

20 cars from Tesla's own used inventory and from cars.com, ranked on one number: price for battery left, meaning dollars for each mile of range the battery should give today. Lower is better. #1 is the benchmark; anything within 5% of it is yellow. Dealer quality first: only cars.com dealers rated 4.0 stars or higher are shown. Every car shows its battery check and a monthly payment. Cars past 175,000 miles stay on the Under $15k list instead. Read it with the trade-off in mind: cheap high-mile cars win on this number; Tesla's own cars cost more per mile but come with a checked clean history and warranty.

The cut clock: how long cars last, and is waiting paying off?

Tesla prices its used cars like a clearance rack. Almost every car is cut a little every day until someone buys it. Then a fresh car takes its place at a fresh, higher price. 12 days of logging every clean Tesla-store Model 3 and Model Y (since Oct 25) show how the clock runs. Every Tesla-store car on this board now carries its own cut clock line.

Price todayTypical cutGone by the next dayHalf are gone withinTotal cut by the time it was gone (cars we saw arrive)
Under $30,000$200 a day (87% of cars are cut on any given day)22 in 1003 days1.0% (1 in 4 were cut 2.4% or more)
$30,000 to $40,000$270 a day (91% of cars are cut on any given day)12 in 1006 days2.2% (1 in 4 were cut 4.4% or more)
Over $40,000$380 a day (85% of cars are cut on any given day)11 in 1007 days1.2% (1 in 4 were cut 3.4% or more)

Is the whole market getting cheaper? Not the same question. This compares the typical (middle) asking price of each car type in the first three logged days with the last three. So far the typical asking price has barely moved since Oct 25 (+0.2%), so waiting alone has not made cars cheaper yet.

Car type at TeslaTypical price at the startTypical price nowChange

Best price for the miles and battery left

All 27 used Teslas on this board, every model and price, ranked on what you get for your money in both ways a used Tesla wears out. Battery: the price for each mile of range the battery should give today. Miles: the price for each 1,000 miles of driving life left, counting a Tesla as good for about 300,000 miles or 20 years, whichever comes first, driving about 12,000 miles a year (so an old car with low miles still loses life to age). Each car gets a score out of 100 on both (100 = the best on the board) and the value score is the average of the two, so a cheap car with worn-out miles and a pricey low-mile car both lose to one that is good on both. #1 is the benchmark and anything within 5% of it is yellow. Only cars.com dealers rated 4.0 stars or higher, and Tesla's own stores.

Under $15,000: ranked by price for battery left

From every used Tesla listed on cars.com nationwide between $9,000 and $15,000 with under 120,000 miles (59 cars, October 25, 2026), keeping only cars.com Great and Good Deals with no accidents reported in their history (checked on each listing; cars with a reported accident are left off, and the Minneapolis Model S came off when its price rose $1,000 above the limit). "Range score" is cars.com's battery-health rating, built from real driving data for that model: Good means the battery has held up about as well as most; Fair means noticeably weaker. Battery warranty is 8 years from the car's first sale, capped at 100,000 miles (Standard Range) or 120,000 (Long Range); every 2013 to 2016 Model S is past it.

How to judge a used Tesla battery

Ask the seller for a photo of the screen at a 100% charge, shown in miles, and divide it by the range when new (listed on every car below). Tesla batteries lose most of their capacity early, then fade slowly: Tesla reports about 12% average loss at 200,000 miles on Model S and X, and early Model 3 data shows under 10% at 100,000. Many reach 200,000 miles on the original battery; 300,000 is possible with noticeably less range.

Range left vs. newRatingWhat it means
90% or moreExcellentBetter than typical for its miles
85% to 90%GoodNormal for 80,000 to 150,000 miles
80% to 85%FairUsable; the price should reflect it
Under 80%AvoidUnless very cheap and you only drive short trips

These bands are a rule of thumb built from Tesla's fleet data and real high-mileage cars, not an official scale. The "expect today" numbers on each car assume normal wear for its miles, minus a little for 2013 to 2016 cars (age) and more for cars cars.com rates Fair. Winter range assumes about 30% less in a Chicago January. Other checks: Tesla's built-in battery health test (Service menu on newer software) or a Recurrent report, and steer clear of ex-Uber or ex-taxi cars that lived on fast chargers unless the range number checks out.

How these are ranked: price divided by the range the battery should give today (the "expect about" numbers in each car's battery check). Lower is better: it is what you pay for each mile of battery left. The #1 car is the benchmark; any car within 5% of it is also yellow. Ranks use the listed price; the Illinois $2,000 rebate is noted on the Illinois car.

The honest picture: at this price you are choosing between a 2019 to 2022 Model 3 with about 90,000 to 110,000 miles, or a 2013 to 2016 Model S with lower miles but no warranty and expensive repairs (an out-of-warranty Model S battery or drive unit can cost more than the car). For most people the Model 3 is the safer buy. Nearly all of these are far away: the only two within an hour score just Fair on battery.

Cybercab watch

Can you buy one? Not yet, and probably not in 2026. As of November 5, 2026 there is no order page, reservation or price on tesla.com.

Latest (November 5): nothing has changed on buying one. Tesla began a show tour of the Cybercab across Europe today (11 cities through January; you can look at it, not ride in it). In the U.S. Tesla says paid Cybercab rides will spread from Austin to Dallas this month, but it has not given a firm date. The federal safety audit below is still open.

Federal audit (November 3): Tesla met NHTSA's October 30 deadline and filed its answers to the 21 questions about how it certified a car with no steering wheel or pedals as legal to sell. It asked NHTSA to keep the answer to one question (number 8, the certification paperwork) confidential, so the public cannot see it. That is a response, not an approval: the audit stays open and NHTSA has not said what it thinks. Tesla skipped the exemption route Zoox used, which caps sales at 2,500 cars a year, and self-certified instead. Until NHTSA accepts that, nobody can buy one.

Federal regulators, the back story: on September 10 NHTSA ordered Tesla to prove, under oath, that the Cybercab meets federal safety rules; Tesla asked for eight extra weeks and got 30 days. Nothing new on pricing, an order page, or Illinois approval.

What Tesla said this week: on its October 21 earnings call, a Tesla engineering vice president said they are "trying" to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of 2026. That is a goal, not a delivery schedule. On the same call Musk said most Cybercabs will be owned by Tesla and run as its own ride service, so early cars may never be sold to individuals at all.

Where it stands: production started at Tesla's Texas factory in April. Paid Cybercab rides started in Austin in early September, by invitation, and Tesla says more cities before year end. Price: Musk keeps saying "under $30,000"; Tesla has published nothing.

Why it is not close for you: it has no steering wheel or pedals, so it can only be sold to the public with a federal exemption (NHTSA proposed a rule change for driverless designs on October 23; a proposal is not approval), and you could only use it where Tesla's unsupervised self-driving is allowed. Today that is a handful of Texas and West Coast cities, not Illinois. Earning money with it also needs Tesla to open its ride network to owners, which it has promised but not done.

What to do: buy the best-value used Tesla now, and treat the Cybercab as a possible second car in 2027 or later. I will flag the day an order page opens.

Model Y or Model 3 for you?

Short answer: get a Long Range AWD (all-wheel drive) either way. Rear-drive Teslas are weaker on Illinois snow and ice, and the Long Range cars also hold more battery.

Model Y: taller seat, easier to climb in and out, a hatchback with far more cargo room (about 76 cubic feet with the seats folded, versus roughly 20 for the Model 3 trunk plus front trunk). Costs about $1,000 to $3,000 more than a Model 3 of the same year and miles, and the ride is a bit firmer on 20-inch wheels.

Model 3: cheaper, sportier, a little farther per charge on the same battery because it is lower and lighter, and the sedan trunk is fine for groceries and luggage but not for bulky items.

Rule of thumb: if you ever haul bikes, big boxes or luggage for a family, pay the extra for the Model Y. If it is mostly you and a passenger, the Model 3 is the better dollar. Both use the same charging network and the same winter range loss (about 25 to 30 percent in January).

Full new lineup today: Model 3 $38,630 to $56,630, Model Y $41,630 to $59,630. New gets you the full 4-year/50,000-mile warranty, a Tesla loan at about 2.49% on Model Y trims (it was 1.99% until October 31), and your choice of color. Used gets you the first $4,000 to $19,000 of depreciation paid by someone else.

Lease vs. buy, in plain numbers

PathWhat you pay over 3 yearsWhat you have after 3 years
Lease new Model Y Standard$4,194 down + 36 × $499 = $22,158Nothing. You hand it back (or buy it at the fixed buyout price).
Buy used 2023 Model Y Long Range (Silver Spring, $31,200)About $12,000 of value lost + about $4,500 interest at a typical 7% used-car rate = about $16,500A car worth roughly $19,000 that you own outright in a couple more years.
Buy new Model Y Standard at 2.49%About $15,000 of value lost (steep year one) + about $2,900 interest = about $17,900A 3-year-old car worth roughly $26,000. The cheap loan is real, but you paid $10,430 more up front than the used car.

Value-loss estimates use Tesla resale curves (a Model Y keeps about 64% of its price after 3 years and about 50% after 5). Treat them as rough, not exact.

Before you buy

  • Illinois rebate: $2,000 back on a used or new EV, bought from an Illinois-licensed dealer (Tesla's Illinois stores qualify; ask for delivery through an Illinois location on an out-of-state car). The window is open now through December 31, 2026, or until the $14 million runs out. You apply after purchase, within 180 days. Household income must be under 500% of the federal poverty line, which is about $160,000 for a family of four, so check that first. Leases are excluded.
  • Seeing it first: Tesla sells used cars online with no test drive, but you inspect the exact car at pickup before signing and can walk away. The Buffalo Grove Model 3 is flagged "available to view" at the store. Book a free test drive of a new Model 3 and Model Y at Tesla Orland Park to learn the car.
  • Financing: Tesla's low-rate loan (about 2.49% now) is only on new Model Y trims. For a used car, get a pre-approval from your credit union before you click Order so Tesla's rate has something to beat.
  • Warranty on a Tesla used car: whatever is left of the 4-year/50,000-mile factory warranty, then Tesla's 1-year/10,000-mile used warranty. Battery and drive unit: 8 years from the original sale (100,000 to 120,000 miles depending on trim). Every row shows the battery date.
  • Winter range: expect about 30% less range in January. Model 3 RWD cars have LFP batteries, which are very durable and like being charged to 100%, but they lose the most range in the cold. The Long Range cars have heat pumps and bigger packs.
  • Skip Full Self-Driving. It's $99 a month if you ever want to try it. Don't pay for it up front.
  • Home charging: budget about $500 to $1,200 for a 240-volt outlet or wall charger in the garage. That's the step most first-time buyers skip and then regret.
  • Illinois EV plates cost $251 a year instead of $151, roughly offset by gas savings in the first month or two.
